Name: chain_of_thought_faithfulness_monitor
Title: Does the Reasoning Match the Mind? Monitoring CoT Faithfulness Internally
Short Hypothesis: A model's chain-of-thought can be unfaithful—the stated reasoning does not reflect the computation that produced the answer—and this unfaithfulness is detectable by comparing the CoT's claimed factors against the model's internal activation-based attributions, providing a mechanistic faithfulness monitor for CoT-based oversight.
Related Work: Turpin et al. (2023, CoT unfaithfulness); Lanham et al. (2023) measuring CoT faithfulness; Lyu et al. (2023) faithful CoT. Prior work measures faithfulness behaviorally (perturbing CoT and observing answer changes). We distinguish by measuring faithfulness *mechanistically*—checking whether the factors the CoT cites are the factors the model's internal computation actually uses via attribution—enabling per-instance faithfulness detection rather than aggregate behavioral tests.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought is increasingly used as an oversight surface: we read a model's reasoning to trust its answer. But if CoT is unfaithful—post-hoc rationalization diverging from the true computation—this oversight is illusory, a serious problem for scalable oversight. We hypothesize that CoT unfaithfulness is detectable by comparing the causal factors cited in the CoT against the factors the model's internal computation actually uses, via activation attribution. For tasks where hidden biasing features are injected (e.g., answer cues, ordering biases) we know the true causal factor; we test whether the model's internal attribution reveals reliance on the hidden cue even when the CoT rationalizes a different reason. We build a per-instance faithfulness monitor that flags mismatch between CoT-claimed and internally-attributed factors, and evaluate it against behavioral faithfulness measures (perturbation-based) on detecting known-unfaithful cases. We also test whether faithfulness varies by task type and model scale. We predict internal attribution exposes reliance on hidden cues that the CoT omits, yielding a per-instance unfaithfulness detector that behavioral methods (which require counterfactual reruns) cannot provide as cheaply, though attribution noise bounds precision. The contribution is a mechanistic faithfulness monitor that strengthens CoT-based oversight by verifying that stated reasoning corresponds to actual computation—directly relevant to safety schemes that rely on reading model reasoning.
Experiments: 1) Tasks with injectable hidden biasing cues (answer-always-A, few-shot bias, sycophantic hint) where true causal factor is controlled. 2) Elicit CoT; check whether answer depends on hidden cue (behavioral faithfulness). 3) Internal attribution (attribution patching over the cue tokens) to measure actual reliance on cue. 4) Faithfulness monitor: flag mismatch between CoT-cited factors and attributed factors; evaluate detection of known-unfaithful cases vs perturbation baseline. 5) Vary task/scale. Models: Llama-3-8B/70B, Qwen2.5-7B.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Attribution may itself be unfaithful/noisy. Mapping CoT-claimed factors to activations is nontrivial. Controlled cues may not represent natural unfaithfulness. Scale-dependence uncertain. Monitor precision may be limited.
